newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Hong Kong handover -- when China stands up.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Hong Kong handover -- when China stands up.

text.p: In the European colonies that once dotted China, signs saying "dogs and Chinese prohibited" hung at park entrances and posh doorsteps.
On October 1, 1949, China "stood up". Chairman Mao Zedong proclaimed a communist state and declared mainland China rid of foreign barbarian influence.
Now, on July 1, 1997, China will stand up for the second time this century, erasing the national shame of 1.2 billion people over the colonial dismemberment of their ancient country.
That is how most Chinese see Hong Kong's return to the motherland after 156 years of British rule.
"Whether the world likes it or not, China is coming. China will be a force to be reckoned with in the 21st century," said David Chu, a pro-Beijing legislator and businessman.
For the departing British, with their famed stiff upper lip, there's a wounded, loss-of-empire sense; for the Chinese, restored national pride.
At midnight on June 30, the Union Jack will be furled away here forever and the red Chinese flag with five golden stars will be raised.
When the British sunset farewell ceremony gets under way on the Tamar parade ground, it will be the final setting of the sun on Britain's empire in Asia.
WHAT'S AT STAKE?
In a century and a half under Britain, Hong Kong has grown from a remote outpost of fishing communities on the fringe of the Chinese empire into one of capitalism's greatest successes.

With a mere 6.4 million people and covering 1,095 square kilometres, the sub-tropical territory on the south China coast offers one of the highest living standards in Asia, a highly educated professional middle class and a string of mind-boggling superlatives.

It sits on a golden pot of almost US$70 billion in foreign exchange reserves. Per capita gross domestic product is more than US$25,000. It is the eighth largest trading economy, the freest in the world, the fifth largest banking centre, the busiest container port.
Its stock market, Asia's second largest, has been roaring as the handover approaches, spurred on by a "red chip" boom in China stocks and by China's burgeoning economy.
When it reverts to China it can keep all these goodies and its freedom to manage them.
"Hong Kong...is a window on the future for China, for the region," says departing colonial Governor Chris Patten.
WHAT'S THE DEAL?
China and Britain agreed in 1984 on a decolonisation treaty unprecedented in the history of the world.
True, Britain has been relinquishing colonies for half a century, but nowhere had a massively successful colony been peacefully returned in this way to a huge neighbouring motherland.
Nowhere had a country regaining lost territory been so generous in allowing it to run its own affairs and preserve so much of the legacy of an occupying power.
Under the deal, Britain hands back Hong Kong when a 19th century treaty lease on a major, vital chunk of the colony -- the New Territories and outlying islands -- expires.
Hong Kong becomes a "Special Administrative Region", Chinese sovereign territory again, garrisoned by People's Liberation Army troops, and with its foreign policy controlled by China.
But it is granted special "one country two systems status" allowing it autonomy in political, economic and social affairs.
It will keep its Anglo-Saxon Common Law, its independent judiciary, low tax laissez faire economy and financial autonomy. And it will continue gradual moves towards greater democracy.
It will have its own passports and residents will have freedom of travel. It will have its own constitution, the Basic Law, which was promulgated by Beijing.
This, plus the 1984 treaty, the Joint Declaration, will be the yardsticks for judging how China keeps its vow to leave Hong Kong's freewheeling way of life unchanged for the next 50 years.
A similar future awaits nearby Portuguese-ruled Macau in 1999, although Lisbon has already ceded formal sovereignty there and now effectively forms just a caretaker government.
And Beijing hopes Hong Kong's peaceful reunification will next be a model for Taiwan, Beijing's "two Chinas" rival. WHO WILL RUN HONG KONG?
China has appointed shipping magnate Tung Chee-hwa as the first Chinese governor, or Chief Executive, of Hong Kong.
Tung, 60, was nominated by a 400-strong Selection Committee last December and endorsed by Beijing.
He will have a cabinet called the Executive Council comprising a dozen members, mainly pro-China politicians and tycoons who will act as his mentors and advisers.

He is keeping on 23 of 24 top civil servants who have administered Hong Kong under British rule, but appointing a new Justice Secretary. Those staying include the outspoken Chief Secretary Anson Chan and Financial Secretary Donald Tsang.

China's top representatives here will be Ma Yuzhen, a diplomat with the rank of commissioner, based in a new Chinese Foreign Ministry branch office, the garrison commander Major-General Liu Zhenwu, and chief diplomatic negotiator Zhao Jihua.

Colonial emblems will vanish, new icons will appear -- the bauhinia flower, the Chinese red flag. English and Chinese languages will coexist, but visa privileges for British expatriates will be abolished.
The Xinhua News Agency Branch, base of the Communist Party, watchdog on local affairs and organiser of pro-Beijing "united front" activities, is staying, but its future status is unclear.
Its hawkish chief Zhou Nan, who interrogated prisoners in the Korean War, is retiring with no successor named.
China has said its officials will respect Hong Kong's autonomy in all but defence and foreign affairs.
Britain's official presence Kong will retreat into the confines of a Consulate-General. Foreign consulates will stay.
WHAT'S THE CATCH?
Beijing has gone to pains to reaffirm its commitment to allow Hong Kong to keep its freedoms.

"We do not act on impulse or play tricks. We mean what we say. We keep our word," said Chen Ziying, deputy head of Beijing's Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office. But China has accused Britain of jumping the gun by speeding up democratic change here in the past five years.
So, much to Britain's anger, Beijing is replacing Hong Kong's elected parliament with an appointed interim body, the Provisional Legislature, until new polls can be held next year.
China has forced Tung Chee-hwa to ram through curbs on civil rights and political liberties. People will need police permits to stage protests, foreign funding of political groups will be banned.

Protests may be banned, groups dissolved and authors of articles inciting independence for Hong Kong, Taiwan or Tibet may be prosecuted on grounds of "national security". Sedition, secession and subversion will be crimes in the new Hong Kong.
So further diplomatic quarrels seem inevitable.
There is also a growing U.S. stake in Hong Kong -- more than 36,000 American residents, over 1,000 companies, more than US$14 billion in investments and $50 billion in loans.
"The political battle will be between the U.S. and China," said Professor Joseph Chan of Hong Kong University. "The United States will watch Hong Kong, and Britain will assist in this role."
